about: Drop-in effects, systems and tools for three.js games. status: ready = copied into blocks/vendor/ and tested; reference-only = we point to the original author's repo at a pinned commit. renderer: webgl2 works with the starter; webgpu and both need three/webgpu (WebGPURenderer); 2d = plain canvas; none = not a renderer thing. See blocks/README.md.

blocks.name: Oil paint
blocks.what: Draws a three.js world as thick oil paint, dab by dab; every stroke is pinned to the world so the paint stays on things as the camera moves. Demo: a snowy ridge under an aurora, and an autumn wood, with a walking character.
blocks.good_for: A painterly third-person or first-person walking game where the look is the point; slow, calm, exploratory games.
blocks.not_for: Fast action with lots of small moving things, phones and weak laptops (heavy), or a look you want to add to an existing scene like a filter: you start from its scene.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs oil-paint

blocks.name: Watercolour
blocks.what: A world that starts as a pencil drawing and is painted in watercolour as you walk through it: the wash spreads from your feet, climbs the trees and stays. Demo: a wood, a stream and a meadow.
blocks.good_for: Gentle exploration games where the player "colours in" the world; storybook looks; a reveal mechanic built into the look.
blocks.not_for: Combat-heavy or fast games; games that need a hard, readable silhouette at a glance; weak hardware.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs watercolour

blocks.name: Coloured pencil
blocks.what: A world drawn in coloured pencil on a sketchbook page: strokes that follow each form, a second pencil for shade, a graphite outline round everything. Demo: a harbour town.
blocks.good_for: Cosy, illustrated, hand-drawn looks; town or village walking games; anything that should feel like a sketchbook.
blocks.not_for: Dark, gritty or realistic games; very fast games; weak hardware.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs coloured-pencil

blocks.name: Patchwork quilt
blocks.what: Makes a world out of cloth: a quilt of puffed patches with real seams and stitches, fuzzy felt, and a tilt-shift camera that sees it as a small thing on a table. Demo: a country sewn into one quilt with a rag doll.
blocks.good_for: Toy-like, handmade, miniature looks; cosy and family games; stop-motion feel.
blocks.not_for: Realistic or dark games; huge open worlds; weak hardware.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs patchwork-quilt

blocks.name: Painted valley
blocks.what: A summer valley in the look of hand-painted animated-film backgrounds: flat clean colour, heaped clouds, painted mountains, brush-mark meadow, and a flat-shaded inked character. Four times of day.
blocks.good_for: Bright, hopeful, hand-painted outdoor games; walking, gliding, farming or adventure games set outdoors.
blocks.not_for: Indoor, dark or realistic games; weak hardware.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs painted-valley

blocks.name: Slice anything
blocks.what: Cut any mesh along any plane, as many times as you like: every piece becomes a closed solid with its own Rapier body, and the cut face shows what the thing is made of (wood rings, melon seeds, marble veins).
blocks.good_for: Sword, knife and slicing games; satisfying destruction of props; physics toys.
blocks.not_for: Games that do not need cutting; huge numbers of cuts per second on weak hardware.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs slice-anything
blocks.notes: Uses three/webgpu (WebGPURenderer). Add ?webgl to the URL to force its WebGL2 path. Pins Rapier 0.19.3 on purpose (0.21 hulls never settle), so it cannot share one Rapier version with impossible-spaces as is.

blocks.name: Impossible spaces (portals)
blocks.what: Portals: join any two rectangular openings and look, walk and throw through them. Rooms bigger inside than out, loops, a door onto a wall, a door that shrinks you to a tenth. The system is one file, src/lib/portals.ts.
blocks.good_for: Puzzle and exploration games built on impossible architecture; non-Euclidean levels; surprise moments.
blocks.not_for: Browsers without WebGPU; games that only need a simple teleport (a fade and a position change is enough).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs impossible-spaces

built_on.name: Wood Floor, Brushed Concrete 04, Marble 01, Black Painted Planks
built_on.by: Dimitrios Savva, Amal Kumar, Rob Tuytel (Poly Haven)

blocks.notes: Needs WebGPU (recent Chrome or Edge). Rendered fine in headless Chromium with WebGPU on.

blocks.name: Grass you can touch
blocks.what: A meadow to the horizon that reacts and remembers: grass bends under feet and anything rolling on it, a scythe mows it and lays the stems in rows, fire spreads with the wind and leaves black ground. A map under it records every touch for your game to read.
blocks.good_for: Outdoor games where the ground matters: mowing, farming, wildfire, tracking, hiding in grass.
blocks.not_for: Indoor games; top-down or high cameras; WebGPU renderers; stylised flat looks without grass; very weak hardware.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs touch-grass

built_on.name: Blade arc model (maths followed, no file copied)

blocks.name: Realistic procedural dungeons
blocks.what: Seeded crypts to walk in first person: vaulted halls, carved columns, sunken basins, worn paving, stairs through arches, candlelight and deep shadow. The layout comes as plain data with room roles and a path grid.
blocks.good_for: Dark first-person dungeon crawlers, horror, stealth; any game that needs many different dark interiors from a seed.
blocks.not_for: Bright or stylised looks; weak laptops and phones (tested on a fast graphics card only); rooms come empty, you fill them.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs realistic-procedural-dungeons

built_on.name: Dirt floor, medieval blocks, medieval wall textures

blocks.name: Fire
blocks.what: Real 3D flames made only in shader math (a ray-marched volume): candle, torch, gas jet, campfire, brazier, fireplace, bonfire, burning crate, fire line, with sparks, smoke and a flickering light in sync. No image files.
blocks.good_for: Any game with fire you can walk around and lean into: camps, torches, braziers, burning props.
blocks.not_for: Huge wildfires across a landscape (use many cheap sprites instead); flat 2D or pixel games; WebGPU renderers or orthographic cameras. Note: it draws the frame itself through its FireLayer (see HOW-TO-USE.md).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs fire
blocks.notes: Inspired by a post by @majidmanzarpour showing volumetric fire in pure three.js; no code came from it.

blocks.name: Realistic car
blocks.what: A car on Rapier at real scale and gravity: tyres that build grip, peak and let go, visible suspension, engine and gearbox, handbrake, and tarmac, gravel and grass. Give it any model with separate wheels.
blocks.good_for: Driving, rally and delivery games that should feel physical; a car to drop into an open world.
blocks.not_for: Arcade kart feel (it is a simulation; tune it down or use a simpler model), 2D games.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs car

built_on.name: Godot Easy Vehicle Physics (gearbox, suspension, assists, ported)
built_on.by: David Shoemaker, Dechode and Baron Wittman

blocks.name: Destruction physics
blocks.what: Breakable structures on the GPU: a timber barn, a steel water tower, a brick wall and a chimney, each hundreds of rigid pieces welded together, knocked down piece by piece by cannonballs. Welds break by load, so things fall the way they should.
blocks.by: Patch (patch.gg), on three-avbd by Steven Bobyn
blocks.good_for: Demolition, siege and catapult games; physics sandboxes; big satisfying collapses.
blocks.not_for: Browsers without WebGPU; phones; games that only need a few boxes to fall (use Rapier). Its physics is z-up; the starter is y-up.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs destruction

blocks.name: Crowds and navigation
blocks.what: Make enemies and crowds walk around any three.js level: build a navmesh from its meshes, spawn people, give them a goal; they flow around walls and each other and re-route when something lands in the way. Small API in metres, groups that arrive and stand, milling, walk/run blending, instanced mannequins.
blocks.by: Patch (patch.gg), on recast-navigation-js by Isaac Mason
blocks.good_for: Enemies that chase, townsfolk, armies, herds, tower-defence paths; any game where many characters must find their way.
blocks.not_for: One or two characters on open flat ground (simple steering is enough); thousands of agents; 2D grid games (use a grid A*).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs crowds
blocks.notes: Its upstream package-lock.json was out of sync with package.json (npm ci failed); we regenerated it with npm install. Nothing else changed.

blocks.name: pixelfx (pixel art effects)
blocks.what: 244 pixel art effects, each a small piece of code drawing into a low-resolution frame: fire, explosions, magic, hits, weather, pickups, UI, critters, and 12 whole acted-out moves. Recolour with palettes, mirror, reseed, export sprite sheets. Includes a Claude Code skill for making new ones.
blocks.good_for: Pixel art and retro games (canvas, Phaser, PixiJS, Kaplay); pixel-style effects on a three.js game via a CanvasTexture or an overlay canvas.
blocks.not_for: Smooth realistic 3D effects (use fire, Effekseer or Ultra Elements).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs pixelfx

built_on.name: Pixel art VFX method and some effects (adapted)

blocks.not_for: Low-poly or flat looks (see lowpoly-tree-generator); thousands of unique trees at runtime (bake a few, instance them).

blocks.name: Adaptive music
blocks.what: A whole adaptive soundtrack synthesised live with Web Audio, no files: electric piano, synth bass, clav, a sax-like lead, strings, vibes and a jazz kit with reverb, delay and tape wobble. A lookahead scheduler and a small conductor follow the game: intensity fills in the drums, danger switches to a tension vamp, progress and checkpoints move through an arc of sections, airtime opens the sound up, pickups play stingers in key, a win resolves into an outro and a loss tape-stops into silence.

blocks.name: Arcade flight (mouse aim)

The player points the mouse and an autopilot banks and pulls toward it; bots use the same autopilot. The camera looks along the aim, with loose sideways springs, a third of the bank and a FOV that punches on boost.

blocks.name: Archery aim
blocks.what: Bow shooting that feels fair from a moving mount: hold to draw, let go, and the arrow goes where the crosshair was. The launch is solved through gravity and drag (a closed form) counting the shooter's and the target's speed; near an enemy the shot locks on and the arrow is steered in flight at a capped rate; arrows test their whole path against moving targets, stick in what they hit and ride it as it falls; thousands of volley arrows fly on the GPU with the same maths; every arrow leaves a short bright streak.
blocks.use_when: the player shoots arrows, spears, thrown objects or other slow projectiles, especially from a moving horse, vehicle or boat at moving targets, and aiming should feel immediate and fair, or the scene needs huge arrow volleys

blocks.name: Blink input (webcam eyes and look-away)
blocks.what: Turns the webcam into a controller: eyes closed (both eyes to close, either eye to open, so squints and winks never count), looking away (head turned, face out of frame, tab hidden, each with a grace time so slow trackers don't flicker) and a coarse left/centre/right gaze, as clean events (blindStart/blindEnd, eyesClosed/eyesOpened, lookAwayStart/End). An 8-second calibration fits the thresholds to each player's own eyes. Falls back to holding Space or an on-screen button, with simulated blinks when there is no camera, and drops to that fallback if the camera dies mid-game. Includes a scripted synthetic face for bots and tests. MediaPipe runs locally; no video leaves the device.
blocks.use_when: the game is played with the player's eyes or face: blinking, closing the eyes, looking away from the screen or turning the head (for example 'it only moves when you can't see it').

blocks.name: Crowd renderer: thousands of animated riders and animals
blocks.what: Draws thousands of animated, skinned horses and riders (or any rigged model: herds, flocks, people) in a few draw calls. Every clip is baked once into a float texture of bone matrices and instances are skinned in the vertex shader (24 floats per instance, no CPU skinning), with clip cross-fades, the body bent along its path, per-instance tints, variant parts and three LODs plus a far one made at load. A rider reads its horse's saddle bone in the shader, so it never drifts off. Comes with a horse, an archer and a knight built entirely in code (no model files) and the horse movement law, so the demo army moves honestly.

blocks.not_for: a few hero characters seen up close (use three's normal SkinnedMesh and AnimationMixer); physics ragdolls; WebGPU projects; models with more than 4 bone influences per vertex or very many bones (the bone texture is one row per frame, 3 texels per bone)

blocks.name: Glider flight (lift, stall, thermals)
blocks.what: A hang glider's flight model: the pilot sets angle of attack and bank, lift grows with airspeed squared, drag has parasitic and induced parts, the wing stalls when slow and nose-high, a g limit caps pull-ups. The air moves: a gusty breeze, thermals that lean and breathe, ridge lift on windward slopes, sink over water. Skimming low is efficient (ground effect and a skim cushion); a flare past the stall is the landing. An autopilot flies scripted routes with the player's inputs and runs in Node to prove a level is flyable. Also a lighter arcade kite mode that never stalls.
blocks.use_when: the player flies, glides or soars without an engine (hang glider, paraglider, bird, wingsuit, paper plane, kite) and height for speed, lift, stall, finding rising air and landing should matter

third_party.author: three.js authors

Kite mode covers fast, forgiving racing flight through lanes, with boosts, slipstreams and wall scrapes that cost speed instead of ending the run.

blocks.name: Hand controls (webcam gestures)
blocks.what: Play with bare hands in front of a webcam. One call opens the camera and runs Google's MediaPipe hand tracker in the browser (GPU with CPU fallback), mirrors it like a selfie and smooths it with a One Euro filter. Per hand you get a stable pose out of 20 (open, fist, point, pinch, OK, V, thumbs up and down, rock, gun, claw...), a score for every pose, palm position, pinch, openness, roll and depth, and events: swipes, push and pull, circles, wave, twist, pinch tap and double tap, throw, hold, and two-hand clap, zoom and steering wheel. Gestures can be switched on and off. Synthetic hands drive the same engine without a camera, for tests, bots and mouse or touch fallbacks. Includes pinch-click and open/fist helpers with hysteresis and plain-words camera error messages.
blocks.use_when: the player controls the game with their bare hands through a webcam: pointing, pinching, making a fist, swiping, throwing or clapping

Comes with a sky that melts into the same haze at the horizon, a warm key + cool fill light rig, drifting cloud shadows, reflections from the sky, and a measured final grade (Khronos Neutral tone map, contrast, saturation, sharpen, vignette, grain, faint bloom, sun shafts, an edge streak for speed).

blocks.name: Photoreal camera and HDRI lighting

blocks.name: Pixel 3D (palette-exact pixel art for three.js, with sprites made in code)
blocks.what: Draws a three.js scene as real pixel art: 12 art pixels per world unit in a small render target, an orthographic camera (side-on or 2:1 dimetric) snapped to whole art pixels, nearest-neighbour blow-up at a whole-number zoom with a sub-pixel offset so panning stays smooth, and no tone mapping, so every screen pixel is an exact colour from one hand-tuned, hue-shifted palette. Meshes are lit through palette ramps (normal lights and shadow maps still work), with optional 1 px depth outlines, world-locked dither and a dithered palette sky. Includes a sprite generator that builds shaded, outlined pixel sprites from shapes (beetles in 16 headings, grubs, crystals, mushrooms, 13 curios, butterflies, birds, leaves) and a rasteriser to draw your own, plus pixel billboards and blink-out pixel particles.
blocks.use_when: the game should look like crisp hand-made pixel art (isometric/dimetric 3D or side-on 2D) built in three.js, with an exact limited palette and sprites generated in code instead of drawn by hand

third_party.what: hash12 / hash22 GLSL hash ("Hash without Sine")
third_party.author: Dave Hoskins

blocks.good_for: Pixel-art games in three.js: isometric/dimetric tactics, farming, dungeon or town scenes from simple meshes; side-on 2D games drawn with shaders; any game that needs many small sprites (creatures, items, pickups) without an artist; games that want one strict palette.
blocks.not_for: Perspective or free-look 3D cameras (pixels can't stay stable), photoreal or painterly games, pixel effects on top of a smooth 3D look (use pixelfx or the PS1 look instead).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-pixel-3d

blocks.name: Procedural songs
blocks.what: Whole songs from a seed with no sound files: a hook melody over 4-bar chord progressions, drums, bass, arpeggio, pad and lead synthesised with Web Audio; menu, game, tense and results arrangements in one key; an intensity value that layers instruments in and out, opens the filter and lifts the tempo; a beat-quantised crossfade to a tense minor version.
blocks.use_when: the game wants background music that never repeats and rises with tension or game phase, without audio files or paid generated tracks
blocks.good_for: Upbeat arcade, party and casual games with rounds: a new song each round, tension that builds, a sudden-death switch, a results jingle. Also a seeded title theme.
blocks.not_for: Calm, sad, orchestral or horror scores without rewriting its progressions and voices; games that need a specific composed track; anything that must sound like real instruments. Nobody has judged by ear how it sounds: listen before shipping.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-procedural-songs

blocks.name: PS1 look (vertex snap, affine textures, low-res dither, blink and dread effects)
blocks.what: Draws a three.js scene like a PlayStation 1 game: 320 x 240 with a 4:3 letterbox, vertices snapped to the pixel grid, affine (warping) textures on normal lit materials, 20 colour levels with 4x4 Bayer dither, a green-sepia horror grade, grain and vignette. Also has eyes-closed blackout with a fading afterimage, eyelids, flash, chunky shake, a vignette punch and 'dread' (swimming rows, colour split). Includes eight tiny procedural textures.
blocks.use_when: the game wants a retro PS1 / PSX, low-poly 90s 3D or lo-fi horror look, or blink / eyes-closed / jump-scare screen effects

third_party.what: hash12 'Hash without Sine' shader function
third_party.author: Dave Hoskins

blocks.good_for: Retro 3D and horror games, first-person exploration, anything built from simple low-poly shapes and tiny textures; converting the starter's meshes in one line with patchPS1Material. Cheap: the scene is drawn at 320 x 240.
blocks.not_for: Smooth modern or painterly looks, 2D pixel art (use pixelfx or meticulai-pixel-3d), WebGPU games, or scenes with huge unsubdivided floors (affine warp tears them).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-ps1-look, then replace renderer.render with PS1Pipeline.render and patch materials (HOW-TO-USE.md)

blocks.name: Ripple water
blocks.what: Water you can touch: a GPU wave simulation (half-float ping-pong, 9-point stencil for round rings, reflective shore) disturbed by one-off drops and by bodies held in the surface, which dimple it when still and leave a real V-shaped wake when moved. The surface refracts the scene under it through the ripple slopes with slight dispersion, catches sky sheen and sun glints on ripple flanks, lights crests and shades troughs, and the bed gets caustics focused by the live ripples plus depth absorption. Splash foam rings and touch/hover markers included. Quality presets keep wave speed constant.
blocks.use_when: the player touches, stirs, drags or drops something into water and the water must answer physically (ponds, puddles, fountains, bathtubs, magic pools, a cursor over water)

third_party.what: GLSL hash12 / hash22 ('Hash without Sine') in src/glsl.js
third_party.author: David Hoskins

blocks.good_for: Ponds, fountains, bathtubs, puddles and pools seen from above or at an angle, where touching or dropping things in is part of the play; calm games; anything with a cursor or finger over water.
blocks.not_for: Open sea, big waves or boats at speed (use an FFT ocean such as ultra-water); water seen from below; scenes with several water levels; WebGPU renderers. It needs a second render pass of the scene (the under-water view), so it draws the frame itself (see HOW-TO-USE.md).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-ripple-water

blocks.name: Riso print look (with a live look switch)
blocks.what: Draws a three.js game as a risograph print: every object renders its ROLE into a small G-buffer, and one pass prints it as three spot inks (blue, pink, yellow) on paper through rotated halftone screens, with inked outlines, plate misregistration that grows with speed, uneven ink, paper grain, 8 ink sets and screen signals drawn in ink (freeze, dash, focus, hit, death, wipe). Game code asks for materials by role (mat(INK.ENEMY), mat(INK.WALL, MODE.WOOD)), so a look switch can redraw the same game in another look live; a plain lit look is included.
blocks.use_when: the game wants a printed, risograph, halftone, zine or screen-print look, or one game should offer several interchangeable visual styles chosen in settings.
blocks.good_for: Indoor or arena 3D games, first-person or third-person, where a strong graphic identity matters more than realism; games where colour must carry meaning (danger pink, yours yellow); offering a 'Look' choice in settings.
blocks.not_for: Adding onto an existing game's PBR materials without touching them (every material must come from mat()), orthographic cameras without a small change, photoreal games, games recorded mostly as small video clips (halftone dots bloat video).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-riso-print, then follow HOW-TO-USE.md: create a look switch on ctx.view.renderer, give every mesh looks.mat(role, mode), and route the starter's draw through looks.view.render.

blocks.name: Rope and cloth chains
blocks.what: Short verlet chains pinned at one end to a moving point and simulated in world space, so scarves, ribbons, hair, sashes, tails, banners and short ropes trail every motion, swing past, flutter in wind and drag on the floor. 2D (with a Canvas brush-stroke outline) and 3D (with a three.js tapered ribbon mesh), plus the tuned presets a 2D fighting game's characters wear.
blocks.use_when: a character, creature, vehicle or prop needs follow-through (scarf, cape tails, hair, ribbons, tail, antennae, banner, a dangling rope) that trails its movement without hand animation

third_party.what: three.js (npm, for src/ribbon-mesh.js and the demo)
third_party.author: three.js authors

blocks.good_for: scarves, ribbons, hair, ponytails, sashes and tails on players and creatures (2D or 3D); kite and balloon strings; banners on vehicles; a dangling rope or chain with a weight; cheap follow-through on many characters at once
blocks.not_for: full cloth sheets (capes, flags, curtains that fold: use a cloth grid); ropes the player swings on or that hold weight against the world; anything that must collide with the body or level (only a flat floor is handled)
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-rope-cloth-chains, then import Chain3/PRESETS/scaled from vendor/meticulai-rope-cloth-chains/src/index.js and RibbonMesh from src/ribbon-mesh.js; step each chain every frame with its world pin; see HOW-TO-USE.md

blocks.name: Sand trails
blocks.what: Soft ground that remembers, simulated on the GPU in a small square that follows a moving body: a groove with berms and a bow wave, craters with rims on landing, water wicking sideways into dry grains with a ragged front, dry sand slumping back past its angle of repose in seconds while wet sand holds for most of a minute, plus a long coarse damp trail. A patch for any MeshStandardMaterial draws it as normal detail with self-shadowing in a low sun and wet darkening. Visual only: physics and ground mesh untouched.
blocks.use_when: something moves over a soft surface (sand, snow, mud, wet ground) and should leave a trail, groove, crater or footprints that fade

third_party.what: GLSL hash12 ('Hash without Sine') in src/sand-map.js
third_party.author: David Hoskins

blocks.good_for: A ball, drop, sled, animal or player crossing a desert, beach, snowfield or mud flat, seen from a chase or top-down camera; anything where the path you took should show on the ground.
blocks.not_for: Steep or overhanging ground (it is a square in x/z); trails that must last for the whole level (the fine map is 12 m and scrolls; the long map is 44 m); gameplay that needs the dents to be solid (it is visual only); WebGPU renderers.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-sand-trails

blocks.name: SDF meshes and caves
blocks.what: Model smooth organic shapes in code as signed distance fields (spheres, ellipsoids, round cones, tubes along curves, boxes, cylinders; smooth union, subtract, intersect, shells, relief) and mesh them at load time with surface nets: vertices projected onto the exact surface, analytic normals, baked cavity occlusion. Plus seeded 3D caves (tubes of open space, domain-warped and roughened) meshed in 24 m chunks by a Web Worker pool and streamed around the player, with collision against the same field.
blocks.use_when: the game needs organic or rounded 3D shapes (creatures, bones, helmets, rocks, blobby props) built in code instead of modelled, or true 3D caves and tunnels that the player moves through

third_party.what: Smooth min/max, ellipsoid and round cone distance formulas
third_party.author: Inigo Quilez

third_party.what: Simplex noise (follows the reference implementation)
third_party.author: Stefan Gustavson

third_party.what: mulberry32 random number generator
third_party.author: Tommy Ettinger

third_party.what: three.js (npm, for geometry.js, streamer.js and the demo)
third_party.author: three.js authors

blocks.good_for: creatures, characters, bones, helmets and props made of blended primitives; rocks and boulders; one-off sculpted pieces; cut-away dioramas; underwater or underground games with real 3D caves, overhangs and shafts; anything that must look smooth without any model files
blocks.not_for: meshing every frame (it is a load-time tool: 0.1-1 s per shape); hard-edged architecture (use boxes); big open landscapes seen from the air (use a heightmap); skinned animation (it makes static meshes; skin them yourself)
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-sdf-meshes, then import from vendor/meticulai-sdf-meshes/src/index.js (no three.js needed) and geometry.js / streamer.js (three.js); see HOW-TO-USE.md

blocks.name: Sonar sketch
blocks.what: A sonar ping that draws the world: 900 rays march outward with the expanding front through any distance/density field and leave glowing points on the walls the moment the front reaches them; the points flash, then cool from teal to deep blue to black over 4 s. Targets in range come back as amber knots, and a hidden big body can be sketched beyond the walls in dim drifting points, faint even through rock. Time-budgeted (2 ms a frame), one THREE.Points ring buffer, fade in the shader.
blocks.use_when: the player navigates darkness, fog or an unseen space by echolocation, radar, scanner pulses or a reveal wave, and the level can be described by a distance or density function

third_party.what: mulberry32 seeded random (src/shapes.js)
third_party.author: Tommy Ettinger

blocks.good_for: Dark caves, deep sea, haunted houses, blind or bat characters, sci-fi scanner pulses: any game where seeing the space is a resource the player spends.
blocks.not_for: Lit, daytime scenes (the points are the reveal and vanish against a bright frame); levels with no field at all (you need at least a rough SDF of the walls); WebGPU renderers.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-sonar-sketch

blocks.name: Tilt-shift macro lens (toy miniature look)
blocks.what: A post pipeline that makes a three.js scene look like a macro photograph of a toy: MSAA HDR scene with depth, ground-truth ambient occlusion, a one-pass gather bokeh depth of field whose plane of focus is tilted into a thin sharp band through your subject (occlusion-aware, cat's-eye bokeh), restrained bloom and an AgX filmic grade with warm white balance, grain, vignette and lens fringing. Quality presets and automatic resolution and preset step-down keep it running on phones.
blocks.use_when: the game should look like a photographed miniature, toy, tabletop model or diorama, or needs a filmic depth of field and grade with phone-friendly quality presets

third_party.what: Single-pass gather bokeh technique (reimplemented, no code copied)
third_party.author: Dennis Gustafsson

third_party.what: hash12 (Hash without Sine)
third_party.author: Dave Hoskins

third_party.what: GTAOPass, UnrealBloomPass, FullScreenQuad, RoomEnvironment (imported from the three package)
third_party.author: three.js authors

blocks.good_for: Toy, marble, tabletop, miniature-city, diorama and model-railway games; any third-person or orbit-camera 3D game that wants a photographic, filmic finish; menus and flyovers that should look like a product shot.
blocks.not_for: Pixel, flat or painted looks; fast first-person games where blur hides threats; orthographic cameras; WebGPU renderers.
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-tilt-shift-macro, then replace renderer.render with lens.render(dt) through a drawWith hook in my-game/src/render/renderer.js and call lens.focusOn(player.position, 'play') each frame (see HOW-TO-USE.md).

blocks.name: Tuning panel
blocks.what: A side panel of live sliders, switches, choices and colours for every feel number in the game, with the game's own value beside each, changed values marked in gold, reset per value, per group or all, search, folding groups, A/B/C slots to compare feels, presets with descriptions, a plain-words short list, freeze and frame step, values kept across reloads, and a one-click hand-back to the agent: Save for my agent (writes src/tuning.json) or Copy changes (a header line plus compact JSON). A drop-in upgrade for the kit starter's own panel.
blocks.use_when: a person will tune the game's feel by playing it and should hand the exact numbers back to the agent instead of describing them
blocks.from_game: TUMEN, Hezarfen, Inkbound, Scrapfall, Still Life 2
blocks.good_for: Any game where feel matters and a person plays between agent rounds: movement, jumps, camera, hit-stop, difficulty, colours. Replaces the starter's panel with the same tuning.json and save endpoint; also works in any page with or without three.js.
blocks.not_for: Settings menus for players (it is a developer tool, English only, shown on the dev server and ?test=1 pages); values that need a reload to apply (it changes them live).
blocks.how_to_add: node tools/blocks/add.mjs meticulai-tuning-panel, then replace my-game/src/core/settings.js with the three lines in HOW-TO-USE.md
